title: Rainhill and the Opening Day, 1829–1830
subtitle: The Liverpool & Manchester Railway: the locomotive trials at Rainhill and the opening of the first inter-city passenger line, 1829–1830
intro: In the spring of 1829 the Liverpool & Manchester Railway had a line almost built and no settled way to move trains along it. Two respected engineers, James Walker and John Rastrick, had toured the colliery railways of the North-East and reported that ropes wound by fixed engines in engine-houses along the route would be cheaper than locomotives. The directors chose not to decide on paper. They offered £500 for a locomotive that could meet set conditions, and in October 1829 five machines came to a level stretch at Rainhill to try for it.

The trials are recorded unusually well, because they were a test with rules. Rastrick, one of three judges, kept a notebook of weights and timings; the Mechanics' Magazine and the Liverpool papers reported every day; the Stephensons and their rival Timothy Hackworth left letters. The figures do not always agree, and the press did not pick the winner: the light London engine Novelty, built by John Braithwaite and John Ericsson, was the crowd's favourite. Rocket, built by Robert Stephenson with a many-tubed boiler suggested by the company's treasurer Henry Booth, was the only engine to finish.

Between the trials and the opening come the first passengers' verdicts. Thomas Creevey, a sardonic Whig, rode in November 1829 and found the speed frightening. The actress Fanny Kemble rode the footplate beside George Stephenson in August 1830 and found it thrilling. Her letter, written the next day and printed in 1878, is the best-known early description of a locomotive ride.

On 15 September 1830 the line opened with the Prime Minister, the Duke of Wellington, as guest of honour. At the Parkside water stop William Huskisson, MP for Liverpool and a long-time supporter of the railway, stepped down to greet the Duke, was struck by Rocket on the adjoining line and died at Eccles that evening. The eyes here saw it from different distances: Harriet Arbuthnot from the Duke's carriage, Charles Babbage from a train that simply stopped, Edward Stanley and Kemble in the procession, and Greville and Creevey through letters and gossip days later. The procession went on to Manchester to a hostile reception from crowds who saw the Duke as the enemy of reform, and returned to Liverpool late at night.

Most of this record is letters, notebooks, newspapers and printed accounts rather than diaries, and the form tags say so. Babbage's memoir was written thirty-four years later, and Mrs Arbuthnot's journal was published only in 1950, so it is paraphrased without quotation. The men who dug the cuttings and laid the line across Chat Moss, and the enginemen who drove the trains (Joseph Locke was on Rocket's footplate at Parkside), left almost no words of their own. They appear in company records and in other people's accounts, not as eyes.
calendar_note: All dates are Gregorian. Weekly papers (the Mechanics' Magazine on Saturdays, the Liverpool Mercury on Fridays) printed reports some days after the runs, and the issue date is shown, not the run date, where they differ. Accounts of the trials disagree on several figures (Rocket's top speed, the length of the timed course); the ledger gives the figures with their sources.

eyes.name: George Stephenson
eyes.role: Chief engineer of the Liverpool & Manchester Railway, aged 48 at Rainhill; self-taught colliery enginewright from Northumberland
eyes.where: On the line between Liverpool and Manchester; on the footplate at the opening
eyes.vantage_label: the line's engineer, on the footplate
eyes.form: dated letters (few); his words otherwise kept by others
eyes.authenticity: George Stephenson wrote little and often dictated. His 1829 letters to G. H. Phipps and Michael Longridge are printed in Pole's Life of Robert Stephenson (1864); much of what he said on the opening day survives only in others' accounts and in Smiles's later biography (1857), which is not a contemporary record.
eyes.bio: The man who had argued for locomotives against the canal interest and the fixed-engine men, and who built the line across Chat Moss. He is seen best through others: Kemble on the footplate, the surgeons at Parkside, and his own terse letters on blast pipes and trial runs.

sources.title: Pole, Life of Robert Stephenson, ch. IX (Grace's Guide)

eyes.name: Robert Stephenson
eyes.role: Engineer, aged 25–27; manager of Robert Stephenson & Co., Forth Street works, Newcastle, which built Rocket
eyes.where: Newcastle works; at Rainhill as Rocket's entrant
eyes.form: dated letters and a printed pamphlet
eyes.authenticity: His letters of 1829–30 to Henry Booth, Michael Longridge and Thomas Richardson survive in part and are printed in Pole (1864) and in later collections; the Observations on the Comparative Merits of Locomotive and Fixed Engines (1830), written with Joseph Locke, is a printed reply to Walker's report.
eyes.bio: George's son ran the Newcastle works and designed Rocket with its many-tubed boiler and exhaust blast. His letters are the working voice of the locomotive side: confident, precise about figures, and quick to rebut the fixed-engine case in print.

sources.title: Pole, Life of Robert Stephenson, ch. IX (Grace's Guide)

eyes.name: Henry Booth
eyes.role: Treasurer (secretary) of the Liverpool & Manchester Railway Company, aged 41 in 1829; Liverpool corn merchant
eyes.where: Company office, Liverpool; at Rainhill and the opening
eyes.vantage_label: the company's treasurer and Rocket's co-entrant
eyes.form: company records and a printed account
eyes.authenticity: Booth's An Account of the Liverpool and Manchester Railway (Liverpool, 1830) is a contemporary printed narrative by the company's own officer, written in the months around the opening; it is partisan for the railway. The company's minutes and premium notices also passed through his hands.
eyes.bio: Booth wrote the company's case and, by his own account and the Stephensons', suggested the many-tubed boiler that made Rocket. He shared the £500 premium with the two Stephensons. His Account is the first history of a passenger railway, written by an insider.

sources.title: Notes and extracts on the L&MR locomotive decision (Tring Local History)

eyes.name: John Urpeth Rastrick
eyes.role: Civil engineer from Stourbridge, aged 49; co-author of the 1829 report on motive power, then a judge at Rainhill
eyes.authenticity: His leather-bound notebook (Science Museum Group, ref. RAST; 18 Sept 1829 to 19 Aug 1833) holds sketches, weights and timings from Rainhill, plus newspaper cuttings. His February 1829 letter to Hackworth survives as a letterpress copy in the Science Museum Group.
eyes.bio: Rastrick toured the North-East with James Walker in early 1829 to judge locomotives against rope-hauled fixed engines, and their report leaned to fixed engines. Months later he stood at the Rainhill posts timing the locomotives, figure by figure. He is the eye of measurement.

sources.title: Notebook of John Urpeth Rastrick (Science Museum Group)

eyes.name: Timothy Hackworth
eyes.role: Locomotive superintendent of the Stockton & Darlington Railway, aged 43; builder of Sans Pareil at Shildon
eyes.where: New Shildon, County Durham; at Rainhill with Sans Pareil
eyes.authenticity: His draft letters and papers were kept by the family and given to the Science Museum (Hackworth-Young gift). The later Hackworth family claim that Stephenson-made parts caused Sans Pareil's failure is a partisan tradition and is reported only as such.
eyes.bio: Hackworth had kept the Stockton & Darlington's engines running and knew their costs better than anyone. He built Sans Pareil largely with his own resources; it ran fast but over the weight limit and broke down. His letters show a working engineman already convinced, in spring 1829, that ropes and fixed engines would not do.

sources.title: Letter, Hackworth to Robert Stephenson, 9 Apr 1829 (Science Museum Group)

eyes.name: The Mechanics' Magazine (reporter at Rainhill)
eyes.role: London weekly for working mechanics, edited by J. C. Robertson; its reporter covered every day of the trials
eyes.authenticity: Weekly issues of October 1829 carried day-by-day reports; the magazine openly favoured the London engine, Novelty, and printed Braithwaite and Ericsson's withdrawal statement. Issue dates are publication dates, a few days after the runs.
eyes.bio: The magazine spoke for London mechanics and backed Braithwaite and Ericsson's light, fast Novelty against the northern engines. Its reports are the most vivid record of the crowds and of Novelty's dash, and a reminder that the press did not at first pick the winner.

sources.title: Extracts from the Mechanics' Magazine and Liverpool Mercury (Spartacus)

eyes.name: The Liverpool Mercury
eyes.role: Liverpool weekly newspaper (Fridays), founded by Egerton Smith; reported the trials and the opening
eyes.authenticity: The Mercury's reports of October 1829 and of 17 September 1830 were widely reprinted, including in the Spectator; the Liverpool papers were proud of the railway and mostly friendly to it.
eyes.bio: Liverpool's merchants paid for the railway, and its papers watched every step. The Mercury's columns carry the public's view: who seemed to be winning, what the opening looked like from the city, and the shock of Huskisson's death.

sources.title: The Liverpool papers reprinted, Spectator 17 Oct 1829

eyes.name: Thomas Creevey
eyes.role: Whig politician and gossip, aged 61; staying with the Seftons at Croxteth near Liverpool
eyes.where: Croxteth Hall; a guest on a trial run of the line
eyes.authenticity: His letters to his stepdaughter Elizabeth Ord were edited by Sir Herbert Maxwell as The Creevey Papers (1903); dates are Creevey's own, sometimes giving only the day.
eyes.bio: Creevey had sat on the side of the canal interest's friends and enjoyed mocking projectors. His November 1829 ride is the first passenger's-eye report of the new speed, and his September 1830 letter passes on an eyewitness's blunt account of Huskisson's death.

sources.title: The Creevey Papers (1903), Internet Archive text

eyes.name: Frances Anne (Fanny) Kemble
eyes.role: Actress, aged 20, on tour in Liverpool and Manchester with her father Charles Kemble
eyes.where: Liverpool and Manchester; on the footplate beside Stephenson
eyes.form: dated letters (printed later in a memoir)
eyes.authenticity: Her letters to Harriet St Leger ('H——') of August–September 1830 were printed in her Record of a Girlhood (1878). The letters are contemporary; the connecting narrative of the book was written nearly fifty years later and is marked as such here.
eyes.bio: A star of Covent Garden who fell, as she put it, half in love with George Stephenson and his engine. Her letter of 26 August 1830 is the most famous early description of riding a locomotive; three weeks later she was on the opening train.

sources.title: Record of a Girlhood, Project Gutenberg #16478
Science and Industry Museum blog: Fanny Kemble

eyes.name: Arthur Wellesley, 1st Duke of Wellington
eyes.role: Prime Minister, aged 61; guest of honour at the opening
eyes.where: In the state carriage of the Northumbrian's train
eyes.authenticity: His letters of September 1830, including a note to the Mayor of Liverpool written from near Roby on the morning after the opening, are cited in modern accounts of the day; his remarks at Parkside survive only in others' reports.
eyes.bio: The victor of Waterloo and an unpopular Prime Minister among Manchester's radicals. Huskisson, whom he had pushed out of the cabinet in 1828, came to his carriage to make peace moments before the accident.

sources.title: The Peel Web: the death of Huskisson

eyes.name: Harriet Arbuthnot
eyes.role: Political hostess, aged 37; Wellington's close friend and confidante, travelling in his party
eyes.where: In the Duke's carriage at Parkside
eyes.authenticity: Her journal was published in 1950 (The Journal of Mrs Arbuthnot, ed. Francis Bamford and the Duke of Wellington); as a twentieth-century publication it is summarised here without quotation.
eyes.bio: Mrs Arbuthnot kept a political journal of the Wellington years. At Parkside she was a few yards from where Huskisson fell, and her account is one of the closest eyewitness records from inside the Duke's own party.

sources.title: Account of the opening, citing Arbuthnot (Cavacopedia mirror of the Wikipedia article)

eyes.name: Charles Cavendish Fulke Greville
eyes.role: Clerk of the Privy Council, aged 36; racing man and diarist
eyes.where: London, Newark and Chatsworth; not at the opening
eyes.vantage_label: at a distance, hearing the news
eyes.authenticity: The Greville Memoirs were published from 1874 in edited form (Reeve), later in full; entries carry place and date headings.
eyes.bio: Greville was not on the line, but his diary catches how the news travelled through the political class: a presentiment beforehand, the details of Wilton's tourniquet afterwards, and Huskisson's last words heard at Chatsworth from Lord Granville.

sources.title: Greville Memoirs, vol. II ch. XII (The Peel Web)

eyes.name: Charles Babbage
eyes.role: Mathematician, aged 38; Lucasian Professor at Cambridge; invited guest at the opening
eyes.where: In one of the trains following the Duke's
eyes.authenticity: Passages from the Life of a Philosopher (1864) recalls the opening thirty-four years afterwards; it is a memoir, not a diary, and dates are inferred from the narrative.
eyes.bio: Babbage met Huskisson the day before and watched the trains halt at Parkside without knowing why. He came away thinking about safety: deflector plates, cow-catchers and ways to cut an engine loose, which he proposed to the directors and which they politely declined.

sources.title: Passages from the Life of a Philosopher, ch. 25 (Standard Ebooks)

eyes.name: Rev. Edward Stanley
eyes.role: Rector of Alderley, Cheshire, aged 51; later Bishop of Norwich; a passenger in the procession
eyes.where: In one of the following trains, Liverpool to Manchester and back
eyes.vantage_label: the passenger who wrote it up
eyes.authenticity: His anonymous account of the opening appeared in Blackwood's Edinburgh Magazine, vol. 28 (1830), pp. 823–830, and is attributed to him in modern scholarship.
eyes.bio: Stanley rode the whole long day and wrote it up for Blackwood's within weeks. He gives the crowd at Manchester and the slow, dark return to Liverpool, with sparks from the engines lighting the carriages.

sources.title: Paul Fyfe, 'On the Opening of the Liverpool and Manchester Railway, 1830' (BRANCH)

entries.headline: Rastrick asks Hackworth what locomotives really cost
entries.digest: Preparing his report for the Liverpool directors, Rastrick wrote to Hackworth at Shildon for the yearly cost of repairing the Stockton & Darlington engines, and for coal and water figures from a test of the Royal George. He wanted each engine's number and the names of its drivers so he could tell the machines apart. He also noted that wrought-iron tyres at Killingworth had shown no wear after nine months.
entries.source_note: Letterpress copy, Science Museum Group 1934-697.

entries.headline: Walker and Rastrick lean towards fixed engines
entries.digest: After touring the North-East, Rastrick and James Walker reported to the directors that rope haulage by fixed engines placed along the line would work out cheaper per ton than locomotives, though they called the choice finely balanced. Booth's later summary gave 6.40d per ton over thirty miles for fixed engines against 8.36d for locomotives. The report left the directors uneasy rather than decided.
entries.source_note: Report of James Walker and J. U. Rastrick (Liverpool, 1829), as summarised in Tring Local History notes; month only.

entries.headline: Hackworth tells Robert Stephenson ropes will not do
entries.digest: In a three-page draft letter to Robert Stephenson at Liverpool, Hackworth set out what different locomotives could pull and argued that stationary engines and endless ropes would be ineffective on the Liverpool & Manchester. The two men were colleagues in the northern engine world and would be rivals at Rainhill six months later.
entries.source_note: Draft letter, Science Museum Group 1934-704.

entries.headline: The directors offer £500 for the best locomotive
entries.digest: Rather than choose between fixed engines and locomotives on paper, the board resolved to offer a premium of £500 for a locomotive meeting set conditions of weight, pressure and performance. Notices went out in the provincial press; the Birmingham Gazette carried it on 4 May. Booth, as treasurer, handled the company's side of the competition.
entries.source_note: Board resolution date as given in standard histories; Birmingham Gazette notice of 4 May 1829 cited in Tring Local History notes.

entries.headline: A longer exhaust pipe for the coke engine
entries.digest: Writing to G. H. Phipps, George Stephenson reported that he had fitted a longer exhaust pipe to the coke-burning engine, set low in the chimney instead of near its top, and that the Lancashire Witch was doing well. It is a glimpse of the blast experiments that fed straight into Rocket.
entries.source_note: Letter to G. H. Phipps, printed in Pole, Life of Robert Stephenson, ch. IX.

entries.headline: An engine pulls 135 people for Huskisson
entries.digest: George Stephenson told Michael Longridge of a preliminary run along the line for William Huskisson, the Liverpool MP. A locomotive drew about 135 people through the Olive Mount cutting at nine miles an hour, and he was pleased: the engine had done well in front of the man whose support mattered most.
entries.source_note: Letter dictated to Longridge, printed in Pole, ch. IX.

entries.headline: The 'prize of public opinion' to the London engine
entries.digest: The Mercury, like the Mechanics' Magazine, was taken with Novelty. It predicted that the principle and layout of the London engine would be followed in all future locomotives, and said that Braithwaite and Ericsson had won the prize of public opinion even if Rocket won the premium.
entries.quote: the grand prize of public opinion
entries.source_note: Liverpool Mercury, October 1829, as quoted on Spartacus; exact issue not confirmed.

entries.headline: Novelty darts off before the crowd
entries.digest: On the first day, with a crowd of thousands along the level at Rainhill, the London engine Novelty ran light and was timed over a mile in under two minutes. The reporter called its motion uniform and steady and gave its speed as twenty-eight miles an hour. A bellows leather then burst and it had to stop.
entries.quote: darted off at the amazing velocity of twenty-eight miles an hour
entries.source_note: Mechanics' Magazine, issue of 10 Oct 1829 (quoted on Spartacus); Rolt's day-by-day summary.

entries.headline: Rocket is shown, but not yet tried
entries.digest: Rocket ran demonstration trips: light at about twenty-four miles an hour, and with a carriage-load of some seventeen tons at just over ten. The judges did not start its formal trial that day but set it for the Thursday morning. Sans Pareil's boiler was leaking and Hackworth asked for more time; Perseverance had been damaged on the road.
entries.source_note: Rolt's results; Tring Local History notes; Pole ch. IX (crowd of 10,000–15,000).

entries.headline: Rain and mud halt the trials
entries.digest: The Liverpool papers reported that Novelty drew a load of three times its weight and seemed as good at hauling as at running light. Then wet weather clogged the rails with mud, and the trials stopped before half the day was over. The judges used the pause to issue fresh rules: ten trips each way over the course, twice, for every engine.
entries.source_note: Liverpool papers reprinted in the Spectator, 17 Oct 1829.

entries.headline: Rocket's seventy-mile ordeal
entries.digest: Rocket, weighed at 4 tons 5 cwt, raised steam in 57 minutes and set off at about half past ten with two loaded wagons, some 12¾ tons. It ran forty trips over the mile-and-a-half course: the first 35 miles in 3 hours 12 minutes, the second in 2 hours 57 minutes, running in places at 18 to 20 miles an hour and better. It was the only engine to finish the full test.
entries.source_note: Pole ch. IX; Rolt's results; Liverpool papers in the Spectator, 17 Oct 1829.

entries.headline: The judges time Rocket's last run
entries.digest: Rastrick and Nicholas Wood timed the runs from the posts. Rocket's runs quickened as the day went on, from over six minutes on the first eastward trip to under four on the last, which the judges' report singled out for the directors' attention. Average running speed came out a little under fourteen miles an hour, burning about 217 lb of coke an hour.
entries.source_note: Judges' figures as given by Rolt (from Rastrick's notebook and the report); note that Rolt's conversion of the last run (3 min 44 s) to 29 mph does not match a 1½-mile course.

entries.headline: Novelty's fire lit at 9.58
entries.digest: Rastrick's notebook logs the Braithwaite and Ericsson engine to the second: fire lit at 9:58:20, steam up at 10:53, away at 11:00:28. He and Wood timed it between the posts. It made only one run before the joints of its feed pipe failed.
entries.source_note: Rastrick notebook, page for 10 Oct 1829 (Science Museum Group transcription); Rolt's results.

entries.headline: Rocket runs light at thirty-two miles an hour
entries.digest: With its tender detached, Rocket was let out for a fast run, and the Liverpool papers reported thirty-two miles an hour. For the crowd, speed was the show; for the judges, the test with a load mattered more.
entries.source_note: Liverpool papers in the Spectator, 17 Oct 1829; Tring Local History notes.

entries.headline: Sans Pareil runs fast, then runs dry
entries.digest: Sans Pareil was weighed at 4 tons 15 cwt 2 qr, over the limit for a four-wheeled engine, but the judges let it run. Its first trip was its best. It averaged about fourteen miles an hour, burning coke heavily, until on the eighth trip the feed pump failed, the boiler ran short of water and a fusible plug melted.
entries.source_note: Rolt's results; Liverpool papers in the Spectator, 17 Oct 1829.

entries.headline: Braithwaite and Ericsson withdraw Novelty
entries.digest: Novelty started again but its boiler joints gave way on the second run. Its makers withdrew it, saying repairs would take at least eight days and leaving it to be judged on what it had already shown. Hackworth's request for a second trial of Sans Pareil was refused.
entries.source_note: Mechanics' Magazine report as quoted on Spartacus (dated there 14 Oct; the issue date is uncertain); Rolt's results.

entries.headline: The premium goes to Booth and the Stephensons
entries.digest: The judges' report reached the directors and the £500 went to the Rocket's entrants, Robert Stephenson, George Stephenson and Henry Booth. Perseverance had never passed six miles an hour, and Burstall later received £25 for his trouble. The company ordered more engines from Newcastle.
entries.source_note: Tring Local History notes (judges' report date; Standard of 29 Oct); Pole ch. IX; Grace's Guide.

entries.headline: Creevey rides the line and is frightened
entries.digest: Taken out with a party from the Seftons' house, Creevey rode behind an engine at about twenty miles an hour and wrote the same day that the quickest motion frightened him. It felt like flying, he said, and he could not shake off the thought of instant death if the least thing went wrong. Yet he admitted the slower stretches were pleasant.
entries.source_note: The Creevey Papers (1903), letter to Miss Ord headed Croxteth, 14th [Nov 1829].

entries.headline: Answering Walker, and four new engines
entries.digest: Robert Stephenson told Thomas Richardson he was preparing a reply to James Walker's report on locomotive and stationary engines, which Walker was circulating. He added that four locomotives were being built for Liverpool and that he was sure they would beat Rocket.
entries.quote: which I am confident will exceed the 'Rocket' in powers
entries.source_note: Letters to Richardson, printed in Pole ch. IX.

entries.headline: The Observations in print
entries.digest: With Joseph Locke, Robert Stephenson published Observations on the Comparative Merits of Locomotive and Fixed Engines. They conceded that locomotives would always burn more fuel than fixed engines, but argued that flexibility, simplicity and the absence of a chain of ropes and engine-houses outweighed it. The pamphlet closed the argument that Rainhill had begun.
entries.source_note: Observations (1830), quoted in Tring Local History notes; month of publication not confirmed.

entries.headline: Booth's Account of the railway
entries.digest: Booth published An Account of the Liverpool and Manchester Railway, the company's own history from the first surveys through Rainhill to the opening. It argued that the railway had changed how people thought about distance and time, and tried to place Huskisson's death as a tragic accident, not a judgement on the machine.
entries.quote: What was quick is now slow; what was distant is now near
entries.source_note: Booth, Account (Liverpool, 1830); quotation attributed by pittdixon.co.uk; publication month not confirmed.

entries.place: Liverpool to the Sankey viaduct and back
entries.headline: On the footplate with Stephenson
entries.digest: Kemble rode out with a small party and Stephenson put her beside him on the engine. She described the engine as a snorting little animal she wanted to pat, and Stephenson explaining it to her as they went. On the way back he let it out to thirty-five miles an hour and she felt no fear at all.
entries.source_note: Letter headed 'Liverpool, August 26th', describing 'my yesterday's excursion', in Record of a Girlhood (1878).

entries.headline: 'Swifter than a bird flies'
entries.digest: Next day she wrote it all to her friend H——: the cuttings and the viaduct, the speed with the wind in her face, and Stephenson himself, a plain-spoken Northumbrian who told her he could not explain how he would do a thing, but he would do it. She confessed herself horribly in love with him.
entries.quote: thirty-five miles an hour, swifter than a bird flies
entries.source_note: Record of a Girlhood (1878), letter of 26 Aug 1830.

entries.headline: A canal man fears the railway
entries.digest: Greville noted that his brother-in-law Lord Francis Egerton, heir to the Bridgewater canal interest, feared the Liverpool railway would ruin the canal's trade. The line was to be opened with great ceremony on the 15th.
entries.source_note: Greville Memoirs, entry of 9 Sept 1830.

entries.headline: Babbage meets Huskisson
entries.digest: Babbage had come to Liverpool for the opening with W. Wolryche Whitmore, MP. The day before, he was introduced to William Huskisson at the Exchange.
entries.source_note: Passages from the Life of a Philosopher (1864), ch. 25; date inferred from 'the day before the opening'.

entries.headline: The Duke's train sets out
entries.digest: Shortly before ten the Duke arrived to a band and a gun salute. His train, of ornate carriages drawn by Northumbrian, ran on the southern line; seven other trains followed on the northern. The procession left at about eleven, with crowds lining the cuttings and bridges.
entries.source_note: Times as reconstructed in modern accounts of the opening (Cavacopedia mirror of the Wikipedia article); Pole ch. IX (eight trains).

entries.headline: Huskisson falls before Rocket
entries.digest: At the Parkside water stop, about noon, passengers got down despite warnings. Huskisson came to the Duke's carriage to shake hands, and Rocket approached on the other line. Mrs Arbuthnot, in the carriage, saw him fail to get clear: the engine passed over his leg and thigh. She recorded his certainty that he was dying.
entries.source_note: Journal of Mrs Arbuthnot (1950), entry on the opening; paraphrased, no quotation (twentieth-century edition). Exact entry date not confirmed.

entries.headline: Stephenson races the wounded man to Eccles
entries.digest: Lord Wilton tied a tourniquet. The injured man was laid in the carriage that had carried the band, and George Stephenson drove Northumbrian towards Manchester at what was reported as about thirty-six miles an hour, stopping at Eccles. Huskisson was carried to the vicarage of the Rev. Thomas Blackburne.
entries.source_note: Smiles (1857) and Tring notes give c. 36 mph over about 15 miles; Stephenson's own account does not survive.

entries.headline: The trains stop for no reason anyone can see
entries.digest: Back in his seat, Babbage felt the trains halt without any visible cause, then saw a single engine race past on the other line with the Duke's car. Only later did he learn what had happened to the man he had met the day before. As the procession went on through dense crowds, he feared a still greater loss of life.
entries.source_note: Passages from the Life of a Philosopher (1864), ch. 25 (memoir, written later).

entries.headline: The Duke goes on, but will not get down
entries.digest: The Duke wished to turn back to Liverpool, but was told that Manchester's waiting crowds might riot if he did not appear. The train went on and reached Liverpool Road station a little before three. Amid hisses, tricolour flags and banners for the ballot and against the Corn Laws, he stayed in his carriage.
entries.source_note: Kemble's letter of 20 Sept 1830 (Lady Wilton's account); the Times, 17 Sept 1830, as cited by Fyfe.

entries.headline: A sea of people, and a return in the dark
entries.digest: Stanley described the crowd at Manchester as an endless sea of people. The return was a long ordeal: engines coupled together, carriages crowded, rain and darkness, and no lamps. Sparks from the engines lit the carriages as they crawled back; the last trains reached Liverpool at about half past ten.
entries.source_note: Blackwood's Edinburgh Magazine 28 (1830), pp. 827, 830, as quoted by Fyfe; arrival time from modern reconstructions.

entries.headline: Riding in the procession
entries.digest: Kemble rode in the procession with her mother. From her seat she saw the crowds and felt the speed. Like most of the passengers, she learned what had happened at Parkside only in pieces, as the day went on.
entries.source_note: Letter of 20 Sept 1830 in Record of a Girlhood; which train she rode in is not confirmed.

entries.headline: Huskisson dies that evening
entries.digest: Surgeons from Manchester judged amputation too dangerous. Huskisson added a codicil to his will, took the sacrament and said goodbye to his wife. He died that evening, about nine by most accounts (Greville wrote ten). He was sixty.
entries.source_note: Greville, 18 Sept 1830; modern reconstructions of the day; entry placed under Stephenson's eye because he carried him to Eccles.

entries.headline: The Duke cancels the celebrations
entries.digest: Early next morning the Duke wrote to the Mayor of Liverpool from where he had stayed the night, withdrawing from the civic honours and festivities planned for him. The same day an inquest at Eccles returned a verdict of accidental death, and the company began its regular service between the two towns.
entries.source_note: Letter cited in modern accounts of the opening (Cavacopedia mirror of Wikipedia); text not seen.

entries.headline: The Mercury reports the great day
entries.digest: The Mercury gave a full report of the opening: the engineering, the crowds, and the death of the man who had done most in Parliament for the line. It set the accident against the hope that railways would serve the welfare and prosperity of the nation.
entries.source_note: Liverpool Mercury, 17 Sept 1830, as quoted by National Museums Liverpool.

entries.headline: A presentiment, and the tourniquet
entries.digest: Greville wrote that he had felt for days that some terrible accident would happen at the ceremony. He described Huskisson being struck by the other engine, Lord Wilton saving his life for a few hours by knowing how to tie up the artery, and death at ten that night when amputation proved impossible.
entries.quote: Wilton saved his life for a few hours
entries.source_note: Greville Memoirs, entry headed Newark, 18 Sept 1830.

entries.headline: Creevey hears it from an eyewitness
entries.digest: Creevey passed on Jack Calcraft's account of the opening. Calcraft had seen Huskisson meet the Duke, and said he had been feeble in his legs since an old operation and seemed to lose his head at the moment of danger. Creevey's tone is harsh, a political enemy's.
entries.quote: lost his head, as he did his life
entries.source_note: The Creevey Papers (1903), letter headed Bangor, Sept. 19th [1830].

entries.headline: Lady Wilton's account
entries.digest: Kemble wrote to H—— with the story she had from Lady Wilton, who had been in the Duke's carriage within a few yards of the spot. She described the Duke's wish to turn back and the warning of riot that made him go on to Manchester, and the sudden end of the triumph.
entries.source_note: Letter headed 'Manchester, September 20, 1830', Record of a Girlhood (1878).

entries.headline: Last words, from the funeral
entries.digest: At Chatsworth Greville heard from Lord Granville, just back from the funeral in Liverpool, that Huskisson had died without ill-will. When the guns at Manchester announced the Duke's arrival, the dying man had said he hoped the Duke would get through the day safely.
entries.quote: I hope to God the Duke may get safe through the day
entries.source_note: Greville Memoirs, entry headed Chatsworth, 27 Sept 1830.

entries.headline: Eight hundred passengers a day
entries.digest: In the first weeks the company found that passengers, not goods, filled its trains: around 800 a day in October, and roughly 50,000 by early December. Coaches between the two towns began to come off the road.
entries.source_note: National Museums Liverpool summary of early traffic; Booth's Account (1830) for the company's view.

entries.headline: Planet hauls the first heavy goods train
entries.digest: The new engine Planet, from the Newcastle works, drew a goods train of about 76 tons from Liverpool to Manchester in 2 hours 39 minutes, with a top level speed of about fifteen and a half miles an hour. Freight working on the line began that month.
entries.source_note: Tring Local History notes; figures differ between accounts.

entries.headline: Huskisson's presentiment, told at second hand
entries.digest: Months later Kemble passed on a story told in London: before the opening, when friends listed the precautions taken, Huskisson had said that he wished to God it were over. She gives it as hearsay.
entries.quote: I wish to God it were over!
entries.source_note: Letter of 5 March 1831 in Record of a Girlhood (1878); a reported remark, not her own observation.

claims.claim: Walker and Rastrick report fixed-engine rope haulage cheaper: 6.40d vs 8.36d per ton over 30 miles
claims.evidence: Walker & Rastrick report (1829), as summarised by Booth; Tring notes

claims.claim: Directors offer a £500 premium for the best locomotive under set weight and performance rules
claims.evidence: Board resolution; Birmingham Gazette notice 4 May 1829

claims.claim: Locomotive draws about 135 people through Olive Mount at 9 mph for Huskisson
claims.evidence: Letter to Longridge, Pole ch. IX

claims.claim: Novelty, light, timed at one mile in about 1 min 53 s (reported 28 mph); bellows then burst
Brandreth's horse-powered Cycloped: horse on a treadmill moves 5 tons at about 5 mph; ruled outside the conditions
Rocket (4 t 5 cwt, load c. 12¾ t) completes 70 miles: 3 h 12 min + 2 h 57 min; running average just under 14 mph
claims.evidence: Pole ch. IX; Rolt (judges' figures); Liverpool papers

claims.claim: Novelty: fire lit 9:58:20, steam 10:53, started 11:00:28; one run, then feed-pipe joints fail
Rocket, tender detached, reported at about 32 mph
Sans Pareil, overweight at 4 t 15 cwt 2 qr, averages c. 14 mph for 8 trips before its feed pump fails
Novelty's boiler joints fail again; makers withdraw it. Burstall's Perseverance never exceeds 6 mph and withdraws (£25 consolation)
claims.evidence: Mechanics' Magazine; Pole ch. IX; Grace's Guide

claims.claim: £500 premium awarded to Booth and the two Stephensons for Rocket
Passenger trial: Creevey rides behind an engine at about 20 mph
Kemble rides the footplate with George Stephenson at up to 35 mph
claims.evidence: Letter of 26 Aug 1830, Record of a Girlhood

claims.claim: Opening: eight trains; Huskisson struck by Rocket at Parkside, carried to Eccles at c. 36 mph, dies that evening
claims.evidence: Greville 18 Sept; Pole ch. IX; Times 17 Sept 1830

claims.claim: Inquest at Eccles: accidental death; regular service begins
claims.evidence: Modern reconstructions of the inquest; Fyfe

claims.claim: Planet hauls c. 76 tons Liverpool–Manchester in 2 h 39 min, top level speed c. 15½ mph
claims.evidence: Tring notes; figures vary between accounts

convergences.label: Spring 1829: fixed engines or locomotives?
convergences.note: Rastrick's report leaned towards ropes and engine-houses; Hackworth, who ran locomotives daily, told Robert Stephenson ropes would fail; Booth's board split the difference by holding a competition.

convergences.label: The trials open at Rainhill
convergences.note: The London magazine saw a sprint by Novelty; the Stephensons' side saw a careful demonstration of Rocket with a load. The crowd and the judges were watching for different things.

convergences.label: Rocket's ordeal
convergences.note: The engine's makers, the judges' stopwatches and the Liverpool press record the same seventy miles, with figures that do not always agree, as figures from the field seldom do.

convergences.label: Saturday: Novelty fails, Rocket runs light
convergences.note: Rastrick logs Novelty's start to the second and its failure after one run; the papers lead with Rocket's 32 miles an hour.

convergences.label: Sans Pareil and Novelty fall out
convergences.note: Two challengers fail in two days, one through a pump, one through boiler joints. The press stays loyal to Novelty while the premium goes north.

convergences.label: The first passengers' verdicts
convergences.note: Nine months apart, a 61-year-old politician and a 20-year-old actress ride the same line: he finds speed frightening, she finds it thrilling.

convergences.label: The opening and Huskisson's death
convergences.note: From the Duke's carriage the accident was seen at a few yards; from Babbage's train it was a stop without explanation; Stephenson was on the footplate racing to Eccles; Stanley and Kemble saw crowds and triumph that turned to dread.

convergences.label: The news spreads
convergences.note: Within five days the death was in the Liverpool paper, a London diary, a Whig's letter from Wales and an actress's letter from Manchester, each with a different tone: civic grief, gossip, political spite and sympathy.

ties.note: Father and son; George was the line's engineer, Robert built Rocket at the Newcastle works.
Co-entrants for the premium; Booth is credited with the many-tubed boiler idea, and the two corresponded over Rocket's building.
Rastrick wrote to Hackworth for running costs in February 1829, then judged his Sans Pareil in October.
Hackworth's April 1829 letter to Robert argued the locomotive case; at Rainhill they were rival entrants.
Rastrick's report favoured fixed engines; Robert Stephenson wrote the published rebuttal in 1830.
He took her on the footplate on 25 August 1830 and explained the engine as they rode.
Mrs Arbuthnot was the Duke's closest confidante and travelled in his carriage on the opening day.
Greville records Huskisson's last words about the Duke, as told at Chatsworth.
Creevey, a Whig, reported the opening from the opposition's side and with little sympathy for Huskisson's Tory colleagues.
Babbage later sat with Stephenson at the British Association in 1838; in 1830 his safety proposals went to Stephenson's directors.
The magazine backed the London engine Novelty against Rocket throughout the trials.
Her 20 September letter relays Lady Wilton's account of the Duke's wish to turn back.

threads_out.note: John Ericsson, co-builder of Novelty, moved from locomotives to marine engineering: his screw-propeller ships of the later 1830s and the ironclad Monitor (1862) grew from the same London workshop that sent Novelty to Rainhill.
Robert Stephenson, Rocket's designer, opposed the Suez Canal scheme in Parliament in the 1850s; the canal opened in 1869, the same year the American transcontinental railroad was completed.

The 4 ft 8½ in gauge used on the Liverpool & Manchester, inherited from the north-eastern colliery lines, became the standard gauge that Japan adopted for the new Tokaido Shinkansen in 1964, unlike its older narrow-gauge network.
Wellington, the opening day's guest of honour, had represented Britain at the Congress of Vienna in 1815 before Waterloo.
Commodore Perry's 1854 gifts to Japan included a working miniature steam locomotive and track, run at Yokohama: the Rocket's descendants arriving as a diplomatic gift.
